n: Jehu’s son Jehoahaz rules Israel for seventeen years (about 814–798 BC).
He continued Jeroboam’s calf worship, like every king of the north.
In anger, the Lord allows Hazael and his son Ben-hadad to dominate Israel throughout Jehoahaz’s reign.
Jehoahaz pleads with the Lord, and the Lord listens because He sees His people’s suffering. God’s compassion responds even to an imperfect king’s prayer.

f.w: he saw the oppression of Israel

n: The Lord sends a “saviour”—a deliverer, perhaps Assyria’s pressure on Aram, or later Israelite kings—and Israel lives in safety again.

f.g: a deliverer; unnamed here, perhaps Jehoash or Jeroboam II, or Assyria’s attacks on Damascus.

n: Yet the people did not abandon Jeroboam’s sins, and an Asherah pole still stood in Samaria. Relief did not bring repentance.
Israel’s army had been crushed to a tiny remnant—fifty horsemen, ten chariots, ten thousand foot soldiers—trampled like dust on a threshing floor.
His deeds are recorded in Israel’s annals.
Jehoahaz dies and his son Joash (Jehoash) succeeds him.
Jehoash of Israel reigns sixteen years (about 798–782 BC). Kings of the same name rule both kingdoms again.

f.g: also called Joash; not the same as Joash of Judah.

n: He too followed Jeroboam’s sins.
His deeds include a war against Amaziah of Judah, told in the next chapter.

f.w: he fought against Amaziah king of Judah

n: Joash dies and his son Jeroboam II takes the throne. The summary comes early; the story then steps back to tell of Elisha’s death.

f.g: Jeroboam II, a powerful king, not Jeroboam son of Nebat.

n: Elisha lies dying of an illness after a ministry of about fifty years. King Joash weeps, using the same words Elisha once cried at Elijah’s ascension: Elisha has been Israel’s true defense.

f.w: the chariot of Israel, and the horsemen thereof

n: Elisha tells the king to take a bow and arrows—a final acted prophecy.
Elisha places his hands on the king’s hands, showing that victory comes through the Lord’s power.
Through the east window, toward Aram, the king shoots. Elisha calls it “the arrow of the LORD’s deliverance”: Israel will defeat Aram at Aphek.

f.g: a town east of the Sea of Galilee, site of earlier victory.

n: He tells the king to strike the ground with the arrows. The king strikes three times and stops.
Elisha is angry: five or six strikes would have meant total victory; now there will be only three. Half-hearted effort limits the blessings God is willing to give.
Elisha dies and is buried. Moabite raiders came into the land each spring.

f.w: at the coming in of the year
f.g: in the spring, the raiding season.

n: At a burial, mourners see raiders, hastily throw the body into Elisha’s tomb, and when it touches Elisha’s bones, the man comes back to life. Even in death, Elisha’s ministry testifies of the God of life.

f.w: he revived, and stood up on his feet

n: The narrative returns to Hazael’s oppression during Jehoahaz’s reign.
The Lord showed grace and compassion because of His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. The phrase “as yet” hints that exile will eventually come.

f.w: because of his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob

n: Hazael dies, and his son Ben-hadad becomes king of Aram.
Jehoash defeats Ben-hadad three times and retakes Israel’s lost cities—exactly the three victories Elisha foretold.

f.w: Three times did Joash beat him
